prompt: Write a short blog post about a sudden change of plans. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the post only.
final_message:
# The Day the Map Stopped Working

I had everything planned. Three days in the mountains, a packed itinerary, a trunk full of snacks, and a playlist I'd spent two weeks perfecting. The cabin was booked, the trail was mapped, and my friend Dana had already taken the time off work.

Then, at 6:40 on Friday morning, my phone buzzed. The road to the trailhead was closed. A landslide, the message said, and it wouldn't be cleared for at least a week.

I stood in my kitchen, holding a cold cup of coffee and feeling the particular grief of a plan dying. It's a strange feeling, isn't it? Nothing had actually happened to me. I hadn't lost anything real. But I'd spent weeks picturing those three days, and now the picture was gone.

I called Dana. "Well," she said after a long pause, "we have the time off. We have the snacks. We just don't have a destination."

That was the moment things shifted, though I didn't know it yet.

We spread a road atlas across her living room floor, an actual paper one, because we both felt like being dramatic about it. Dana closed her eyes and put her finger down. It landed on a tiny town two hours east that neither of us had ever heard of. It had a name with too many consonants and, according to a quick search, one diner, one lake, and a museum devoted entirely to barbed wire.

"Perfect," Dana said. "Absolutely not what we planned."

So we went. No itinerary, no trail map, no reservations. We found a motel with a neon sign missing half its letters. We ate pie at the diner, where a woman named Marguerite told us, unprompted, exactly where to watch the sunset. We did, from a rickety dock at the lake, with our shoes off and our feet in the cold water. We visited the barbed wire museum, and I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit it was fascinating.

Nothing about those three days looked like what I'd imagined. And yet, looking back, I can't find a single moment I'd trade for the original plan.

I think about that now whenever something falls apart. The plan was never the point. It was just a way of getting me out the door. The landslide simply took the decision out of my hands and handed me something better than I'd have chosen.

Next time my plans collapse, I'm going to try to remember that. I'll grab a paper map, call a friend, and point my finger somewhere I've never been.

The best trips, it turns out, are the ones that never made it onto the itinerary.
